question: In Los Angeles how many schools have more than 500 free meals but less than 700 free or reduced price meals for K-12?

candidates.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM frpm
JOIN schools ON frpm.CDSCode = schools.CDSCode
WHERE schools.City = 'Los Angeles'
  AND frpm.`Free Meal Count (K-12)` > 500
  AND frpm.`FRPM Count (K-12)` < 700

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT s.School)
FROM schools s
JOIN frpm f ON s.CDSCode = f.CDSCode
WHERE s.City = 'Los Angeles'
  AND f.`Free Meal Count (K-12)` > 500
  AND f.`FRPM Count (K-12)` < 700

FROM frpm f

question: Among the accounts who have loan validity more than 12 months, list out the accounts that have the highest approved amount and have account opening date in 1993.

SELECT l.account_id, l.amount, a.date
FROM loan l
JOIN account a ON l.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE l.duration > 12
  AND a.date LIKE '1993%'
ORDER BY l.amount DESC
LIMIT 1

SELECT a.account_id, l.amount
FROM account a
JOIN loan l ON a.account_id = l.account_id
WHERE l.duration > 12
  AND STRFTIME('%Y', a.date) = '1993'
ORDER BY l.amount DESC
LIMIT 1

SELECT a.account_id, l.amount, a.date
FROM account a
JOIN loan l ON a.account_id = l.account_id
WHERE l.duration > 12
  AND a.date BETWEEN '1993-01-01' AND '1993-12-31'
ORDER BY l.amount DESC
LIMIT 1

FROM loan l
JOIN account a ON l.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE l.duration > 12
  AND a.date LIKE '1993%'

      JOIN account a2 ON l2.account_id = a2.account_id
      WHERE l2.duration > 12
        AND a2.date LIKE '1993%'

SELECT a.account_id, l.amount
FROM account a
JOIN loan l ON a.account_id = l.account_id
WHERE l.duration > 12
  AND a.date LIKE '1993%'
ORDER BY l.amount DESC
LIMIT 1

SELECT l.account_id, l.amount
FROM loan l
JOIN account a ON l.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE l.duration > 12
  AND a.date LIKE '1993-%'
  AND l.amount = (

      FROM loan
      WHERE duration > 12

            WHERE date LIKE '1993-%'

FROM loan l
JOIN account a ON l.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE l.duration > 12
  AND a.date LIKE '1993-%'
ORDER BY l.amount DESC
LIMIT 1

FROM loan
JOIN account ON loan.account_id = account.account_id

GROUP BY account_id
ORDER BY highest_approved_amount DESC

question: Write all the comments left by users who edited the post titled 'Why square the difference instead of taking the absolute value in standard deviation?'
evidence: "Why square the difference instead of taking the absolute value in standard deviation?" is the Title of post;

candidates.sql:
SELECT c.Text
FROM comments c
JOIN posts p ON c.PostId = p.Id
WHERE p.Title = 'Why square the difference instead of taking the absolute value in standard deviation?'
result: In a way, the measurement you proposed is widely used in case of error (model quality) analysis -- then it is called MAE, "mean absolute error".

In accepting an answer it seems important to me that we pay attention to whether the answer is circular.  The normal distribution is based on these measurements of variance from squared error terms, but that isn't in and of itself a justification for using (X-M)^2 over |X-M|.
Do you think the term standard means this is THE standard today ? Isn't it like asking why principal component are "principal" and not secondary ?
My understanding of this question is that it could be shorter just be something like: what is the difference between the MAE and the RMSE ? otherwise it is difficult to deal with.
Related question: http://stats.stackexchange.com/q/354/919 ("Bias towards natural numbers in the case of least squares.")

JOIN posts p ON c.PostId = p.Id

result: *"the absolute-value method will be smaller"*, actually, it'll be bigger for small variances - it'll always be closer to 1 though (unless it is 1 or 0)
+1 @whuber: Thanks for pointing this out, which was bothering me as well.  Now, though, have to go and read up on the Central Limit Theorem!  Oh well. ;-)
Despite the antiquity of this question, I've posted a new answer, which says something that I think is worth knowing about.
Do you think the term standard means this is THE standard today ? Isn't it like asking why principal component are "principal" and not secondary ?

Every answer offered so far is circular. They focus on ease of mathematical calculations (which is nice but by no means fundamental) or on properties of the Gaussian (Normal) distribution and OLS. Around 1800 Gauss *started* with least squares and variance and from those *derived* the Normal distribution--there's the circularity. A truly fundamental reason that has not been invoked in any answer yet is the *unique* role played by the variance in the [Central Limit Theorem](http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/3734). Another is the importance in decision theory of minimizing quadratic loss.

question: How many users are awarded with more than 5 badges?
evidence: more than 5 badges refers to Count (Name) > 5; user refers to UserId

candidates.sql:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT UserId) 
FROM badges 
GROUP BY UserId 
HAVING COUNT(Name) > 5

SELECT COUNT(UserId) 
FROM (
    SELECT UserId 
    FROM badges 
    GROUP BY UserId 
    HAVING COUNT(Name) > 5
) AS user_badges

SELECT COUNT(UserId) 
FROM (
    SELECT UserId 
    FROM badges 
    GROUP BY UserId 
    HAVING COUNT(Name) > 5
) AS subquery

WHERE users.Reputation = (SELECT MAX(Reputation) FROM users)

question: What is the name of tags used by John Stauffer's?
evidence: DisplayName = 'John Stauffer';

candidates.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT t.TagName
FROM posts p
JOIN tags t ON p.Tags LIKE '%' || t.TagName || '%'
JOIN users u ON p.OwnerUserId = u.Id
WHERE u.DisplayName = 'John Stauffer'

SELECT DISTINCT T2.TagName
FROM posts AS T1
JOIN tags AS T2
ON T1.Tags LIKE '%' || T2.TagName || '%'
JOIN users AS T3
ON T1.OwnerUserId = T3.Id
WHERE T3.DisplayName = 'John Stauffer'

SELECT DISTINCT T1.TagName
FROM tags AS T1
JOIN posts AS T2 ON T1.TagName LIKE '%' || REPLACE(SUBSTR(T2.Tags, INSTR(T2.Tags, '<') + 1, INSTR(T2.Tags, '>') - INSTR(T2.Tags, '<') - 1), '>', '') || '%'
JOIN users AS T3 ON T2.OwnerUserId = T3.Id
WHERE T3.DisplayName = 'John Stauffer'

    postTags T3 ON T1.Id = T3.TagId
JOIN 
    posts T2 ON T3.PostId = T2.Id
WHERE

question: Describe the post history counts and last edit date of the post title "What is the best introductory Bayesian statistics textbook?"

candidates.sql:
SELECT 
    COUNT(ph.Id) AS PostHistoryCount,
    p.LastEditDate
FROM 
    posts p
LEFT JOIN 
    postHistory ph ON p.Id = ph.PostId
WHERE 
    p.Title = 'What is the best introductory Bayesian statistics textbook?'
GROUP BY 
    p.LastEditDate

question: Among all the posts posted by the most influential user, identify the percentage with a score above 50.
evidence: The user with higher reputation has more influence; DIVIDE(COUNT(stats_posts.Id where Score > = 50 and MAX(Reputation))), COUNT(stats_posts.Id where MAX(Reputation)) as percentage;

candidates.sql:
SELECT 
    CAST(COUNT(CASE WHEN p.Score >= 50 THEN 1 ELSE NULL END) AS REAL) * 100 / COUNT(p.Id) AS percentage
FROM 
    posts p
JOIN 
    users u ON p.OwnerUserId = u.Id
WHERE 
    u.Reputation = (SELECT MAX(Reputation) FROM users)
